\chapter{Synthesis --- You Can Hear Which Past It Is}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-preterito}
\hlchaptermodality{79}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell a regular preterite from a strong one by ear, and say why only one of them carries an accent.}

The accent is the stress written down: ending-stressed regular, stem-stressed strong.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Practice — six singular patterns, no hidden vocabulary}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve only the three singular persons of each learned row. Every word in the short sentences is already known.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter}]
Regular rows:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{yo:} \textbf{hablé · comí · viví}.
  \item \textbf{tú:} \textbf{hablaste · comiste · viviste}.
  \item \textbf{él / ella / usted:} \textbf{habló · comió · vivió}.
\end{itemize}

Strong rows:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{yo:} \textbf{tuve · hice · estuve}.
  \item \textbf{tú:} \textbf{tuviste · hiciste · estuviste}.
  \item \textbf{él / ella / usted:} \textbf{tuvo · hizo · estuvo}.
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{-er} and \textbf{-ir} rows share \textbf{-í, -iste, -ió}. The three strong rows share \textbf{-e, -iste, -o}, but their stems must be learned: \textbf{tuv-, hic-/hiz-, estuv-}. Plural persons, more strong verbs, and new time or setting vocabulary remain outside this checkpoint.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: let spelling show the stress}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Regular \textbf{comí, comió, viví, vivió} carry written accents for final stress.
  \item Strong \textbf{tuve, tuvo, hice, hizo, estuve, estuvo} carry no written accents; stress remains in the strong stem.
  \item \textbf{Comiste} and \textbf{viviste} need no accent because their ordinary stress is already next to last.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The regular \textbf{-er/-ir} endings continue Latin perfect material reshaped across Romance. \textbf{Tuve} and \textbf{hice} continue older strong-perfect histories, also reshaped rather than copied letter for letter. \textbf{Estuve} shows especially clear analogical remodeling beside the \textbf{-uv-} family of \textbf{tuve}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hablé, comí, viví”
  \item “tuve, hice, estuve”
  \item “Hice café. Viví en Madrid. Estuve bien.”
  \item “comí and comió have accents; tuve and tuvo do not”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the regular \textbf{comer} and \textbf{vivir} sets. (\emph{Comí, comiste, comió; viví, viviste, vivió.}) Give the three strong sets. (\emph{Tuve, tuviste, tuvo; hice, hiciste, hizo; estuve, estuviste, estuvo.}) Which rows share endings? (\textbf{-er/-ir} share one regular set; the strong rows share another.) The next chapter can add a new past contrast without borrowing any plural form here.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Synthesis — you can hear which past it is}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-sintesis-preterito}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Say \emph{comí}, then \emph{tuve}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the stress tells you everything}]
Say those two again and listen to where your voice lifts.

\begin{quote}
com\textbf{í} — the stress lands on the \textbf{ending}. \textbf{tu}ve — the stress lands on the \textbf{stem}.
\end{quote}

That is not a detail. It is the whole difference between the two kinds of past in this chapter, and it is audible before you know anything else about the verb.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Endings stressed} $\to$ the regular preterite. It needs a written accent, because Spanish marks a stressed final vowel: \emph{comí}, \emph{viví}.
  \item \textbf{Stem stressed} $\to$ a strong preterite. It needs \textbf{no accent at all}: \emph{tuve}, \emph{hice}, \emph{estuve}.
\end{itemize}

So the accent is not extra spelling to remember. It is the stress, written down. If a preterite has no accent, the stress moved back onto the stem, and you are looking at one of the strong ones.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The two kinds have two histories.

The regular preterite is Spanish doing what Spanish does: one set of endings, and — as in the present and the imperfect — \textbf{-er} and \textbf{-ir} agreeing with each other rather than going separate ways.

The strong preterites are older. They are Latin's own perfect, carried through with the stress where Latin had put it, on verbs used too heavily ever to be rebuilt. Which is the same reason the imperfect has only three irregulars: the words people say constantly are the ones that keep their odd shapes.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{comí}, \emph{viví} — and feel the lift on the last syllable
  \item \emph{tuve}, \emph{hice}, \emph{estuve} — and feel it move back
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until you can place a preterite by ear before you place it by rule.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the stress fall in a strong preterite? (\textbf{On the stem.}) What does a missing accent tell you? (That it is one of the strong ones.) And why do the strong ones exist at all? (They are Latin's own perfect, kept intact on verbs used too much to be rebuilt.)
\end{tcolorbox}
